393.title: Shemini: grief has its reasons (Leviticus 10:16–20)
393.hook: Aaron doesn't eat the offering in his grief; Moses hears him out and agrees
393.howItsDone: In Jewish law a mourner between a death and the burial, an onen, is exempt from many positive commandments, and during shiva the community brings food and leads prayers in the mourner's home so the mourner can simply grieve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aaron's silence. Your line was and Aaron held his peace. Did you wait a breath before answering someone? Today, the same terrible day, and Aaron finally speaks. Day three hundred ninety-three.

A manager notices a missed deadline and walks over, ready to say something sharp. Then the employee says, quietly: my father died on Tuesday. And the manager has a choice. Hold the line, because rules are rules. Or hear the reason, and let it change the answer. The same afternoon Aaron lost his sons, there was still work to do in the sanctuary. One offering was supposed to be eaten by the priests. It wasn't. It was burned instead. And Moses, who has just lost two nephews himself, goes looking for it.
screen: `MY FATHER DIED ON TUESDAY.` → `RULES, OR REASONS?` → `MOSES GOES LOOKING.`

segments.voice: Moses searches. The Hebrew says darosh darash, he searched and searched, for the goat of the sin offering, and finds it burned. He's angry, and he aims it at Aaron's two surviving sons, Elazar and Itamar: why didn't you eat it in the holy place, as I commanded? An old scribal tradition, recorded in the Talmud, counts darosh darash as the middle words of the whole Torah. The center of the scroll is a man searching. Then Aaron answers for his sons. He speaks for the first time since the fire. In plain words: today they brought their offerings, and today such things have happened to me. If I had eaten the sin offering today, would that have been good in God's eyes? He doesn't argue the law. He names his grief, and asks whether a mourner's meal is the kind of holiness God wants. And Moses hears. The text says that when Moses heard, it was good in his eyes. Rashi adds the striking part: Moses admitted it, and wasn't ashamed to say, I hadn't heard that rule. The lawgiver, on that terrible day, says in effect: you're right, and I was wrong. Commentators draw a lesson from it. A law can make room for a mourner. And the person who holds authority can change course after listening. Jewish law still does this: a mourner before the funeral is exempt from many commandments, so the grief can be what it is.
screen: `DAROSH DARASH: HE SEARCHED HARD.` · `AARON NAMES HIS GRIEF.` · `MOSES HEARS, AND IT WAS GOOD.` · `THE LAW MAKES ROOM FOR MOURNERS.` · then, large: `MOSES HEARD, AND AGREED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone grieve their own way. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you love who is carrying something heavy, and handling it differently than you would. Too quiet, too busy, too angry, too much. If a rule in you says they're doing it wrong, notice it. Then, like Moses, hear their reason, even if you have to imagine it. Let it be good in your eyes. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers just as they are. The bell holds the time.
Shemini, the eighth: the portion where Aaron, in his grief, doesn't eat the offering, and Moses listens, and agrees.
Your line: moses heard, and agreed. Today, when someone's choice puzzles you, ask for the reason before you correct it. Day three hundred ninety-three.

394.title: Shemini: be holy (Leviticus 11:44–45)
394.hook: the food laws end with a call: "be holy, for I am holy"
394.howItsDone: Many Jews keep kashrut, the dietary laws drawn from Leviticus 11 and later rabbinic law, and say a blessing before eating and Birkat Hamazon, the grace after meals, after a meal with bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grief had its reasons. Your line was Moses heard, and agreed. Did you ask for someone's reason before correcting them? Today, Shemini ends, at the dinner table. Day three hundred ninety-four.

Open a pantry in an observant Jewish home and look at the labels. Small symbols on the cans and boxes: a U in a circle, a K, a star. Each one says an inspector checked what's inside. It can look like bookkeeping. But those symbols trace back to a long chapter of Leviticus that lists which animals may be eaten: land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, fish with fins and scales, and a long roll call of birds that may not be eaten. And at the end of all that detail, the chapter suddenly stops listing, and gives the reason.
screen: `LABELS ON THE CANS.` → `HOOVES, FINS AND SCALES.` → `AND THEN, THE REASON.`

segments.voice: First, the line. After the animals, the reason comes, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "ye shall therefore be holy, for I am holy." The food laws don't end on hygiene or health. They end on holiness. Second, the word. Kadosh, holy. Its root, k-d-sh, means set apart, marked off for something. You already know the family. Kiddush, the blessing over wine that sets Shabbat apart from the week. Kaddish, the prayer that sanctifies God's name. Kiddushin, the word for marriage, two people set apart for each other. Holy, in Hebrew, is less a glow than a boundary drawn with care. Third, where the boundary is drawn. Not only in the sanctuary, which is where Shemini began, with fire and priests and an eighth day. The chapter ends at the dinner plate. What you eat, three times a day, becomes a place where holiness happens. Commentators have offered many reasons for the specific rules, and the Torah itself gives none beyond this one. Many Jews keep kashrut without needing a further reason: it's how they say yes to the call. Fourth, the everyday. Jewish practice wraps a meal in blessings, one before, another after. A table, the rabbis said, can be like an altar. You don't have to keep kosher to notice what the chapter is doing. It takes the most ordinary act there is, and says: here, too.
screen: `THE LIST ENDS WITH A REASON.` · `KADOSH: SET APART.` · `KIDDUSH, KADDISH, KIDDUSHIN.` · `HOLINESS AT THE DINNER PLATE.` · then, large: `BE HOLY, FOR I AM HOLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one meal today with full attention. Right now, settle, and breathe, and get ready for it. Picture the next thing you'll eat. Where did it grow? Who carried it, cooked it, packed it? When the meal comes, take the first three bites slowly, with no screen. Many Jews say a blessing before eating; if you pray, you can say one you know. If not, a moment of noticing is its own kind of setting apart. The bell holds the time.
Kadosh. Holy: set apart, marked off for something that matters. The root of kiddush, kaddish and kiddushin.
Your line: holy in the everyday. Today, pick one ordinary act, a meal, a shower, a walk to the car, and do it as if it were set apart. Day three hundred ninety-four.

395.title: Tazria: after a birth (Leviticus 12)
395.hook: a new mother's time apart and her offering mark a life-changing passage
395.howItsDone: Jewish communities mark a birth with a brit milah for a boy on the eighth day and a naming for a girl, often at the Torah reading or a simchat bat; in many communities a mother says Birkat Hagomel, the blessing of thanks after danger, when she returns to synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kadosh: holy, set apart, right down to the dinner plate. Your line was holy in the everyday. Which ordinary act did you set apart? Today, a new portion, and a new life. Day three hundred ninety-five.

Ask anyone who has just had a baby how they are, and watch their face try to answer. Exhausted. Overjoyed. Sore. Terrified. Sometimes all four before lunch. The world goes on as usual outside, and inside the house, everything has moved. The next portion of Leviticus is called Tazria, from its opening verb: when a woman conceives. And before it turns to skin and sickness, it stops for one short chapter, only eight verses, to mark what happens to a woman after she gives birth.
screen: `EXHAUSTED, OVERJOYED, SORE.` → `EVERYTHING HAS MOVED.` → `TAZRIA: WHEN A WOMAN CONCEIVES.`

segments.voice: Start with the time apart. After a birth, the mother enters a period of ritual impurity, called tumah, and then days of purification. For a boy, seven days and then thirty-three. For a girl, fourteen and then sixty-six. The Torah gives the numbers and not the reasons, and nobody knows for certain why they differ. Then, what tumah is and isn't. It isn't dirt, and it isn't sin. In Leviticus it comes from contact with the edges of life: birth, death, bodily flows. A priest burying his own parent becomes impure too. Some teachers read the mother's time apart as a recognition that she has just been to the very edge of life and back. It meant, in practice, a stretch of weeks when she didn't come to the sanctuary, and wasn't expected to. Then the offering. When the days are full, she brings a lamb and a dove or pigeon. And then a line that matters: if she can't afford a lamb, two birds will do. Nobody is priced out of marking a birth. The Talmud asks why a mother brings a sin offering at all, and one answer is gentle: in the pain of labor, a woman may swear things she never means to keep. And the passage itself. Birth changes the mother, not only the household. Leviticus gives that change a time, a boundary and a ceremony, so it isn't just swallowed by the week. Today, Jewish communities mark births with a bris for boys, naming ceremonies for girls, and a blessing of thanks a mother can say in synagogue.
screen: `DAYS APART, BY THE CALENDAR.` · `TUMAH: NOT DIRT, NOT SIN.` · `A LAMB, OR TWO BIRDS.` · `A PASSAGE WITH A BOUNDARY.` · then, large: `BIRTH CHANGES EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a new parent. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has had a baby recently, or adopted one, or is about to. Or your own parents, the year you arrived. Think about what that season actually asked of them: the nights, the body, the fear, the joy. Then choose one small thing you could do this week. A meal left at the door. A message that asks how they are, not only how the baby is. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayers. The bell holds the time.
Tazria. When a woman conceives: the portion that opens by marking a mother's passage after birth, with time apart and an offering anyone can afford.
Your line: birth changes everything. Today, ask one parent how they are, and wait for a real answer. Day three hundred ninety-five.

396.title: Tazria: the skin affliction (Leviticus 13)
396.hook: not leprosy as we know it; the rabbis linked it to harmful speech
396.howItsDone: Many Jews study the laws of lashon hara, harmful speech, especially from the Chafetz Chaim's books, and some keep a daily study schedule on guarding the tongue; the portions Tazria and Metzora are often taught as lessons about speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, after a birth: a mother's time apart, and an offering anyone could afford. Your line was birth changes everything. Did you ask a parent how they really are? Today, a chapter that's hard to love. Day three hundred ninety-six.

Leviticus 13 is fifty-nine verses of rashes. White spots, raw flesh, hair turning yellow, patches that spread or don't. It's an easy chapter to skim. Older English Bibles called the condition leprosy, and that word carries centuries of fear. But read closely and something doesn't fit. The same affliction can appear on a wool garment. A leather bag. Later, on the stone walls of a house. Whatever this is, it isn't the disease we call leprosy today. So what is it?
screen: `FIFTY-NINE VERSES OF RASHES.` → `ON CLOTHES. ON WALLS.` → `SO WHAT IS IT?`

segments.voice: Start with the name. The Hebrew is tzara'at. When the Torah was translated into Greek, the word used was lepra, and from there English got leprosy. But Hansen's disease, what we call leprosy now, doesn't grow on fabric or walls. There may be no exact modern match, and Maimonides wrote that tzara'at was not a natural illness at all but a sign. Then the rabbis' reading. The Talmud plays on the word for the afflicted person, metzora, and hears motzi shem ra: one who spreads a bad name. Tzara'at, in this reading, is what harmful speech looks like when it finally shows. They point to a story. In the book of Numbers, Miriam speaks against her brother Moses, and she is struck with tzara'at, white as snow. Aaron pleads with Moses for her, Moses prays, and the whole camp waits seven days for her to return. Later, Deuteronomy tells the people to remember what was done to Miriam on the way out of Egypt. The rabbis heard that as: remember what words can do. Maimonides, following an older midrash, adds an order to all this. The affliction starts on the walls of the house, then the clothes, and only then the skin. A warning, then a closer warning, then the body. Words work the same way: a remark at the edges of a group, then closer, until it sits on someone's skin. Jewish law has a name for harmful true speech, lashon hara, the evil tongue, and whole books on avoiding it.
screen: `NOT THE LEPROSY WE KNOW.` · `METZORA: ONE WHO SPREADS A BAD NAME.` · `MIRIAM, WHITE AS SNOW.` · `WALLS, CLOTHES, THEN SKIN.` · then, large: `WORDS SHOW ON THE SKIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch your words for a day. Settle, and breathe. Think back over yesterday's conversations, the texts, the group chats, the comment you made in the kitchen. Was there a sentence about someone who wasn't there? True or not, notice how it felt to say it, and how it would feel to hear it about yourself. Then choose one person you'll speak about only kindly today, or not at all. The bell holds the time.
Tzara'at. The skin affliction of Leviticus, not the leprosy we know, which the rabbis read as harmful speech made visible.
Your line: words show on the skin. Today, before you repeat something about someone, ask whether you'd say it with them in the room. Day three hundred ninety-six.

397.title: Tazria: the priest must look (Leviticus 13:2–3)
397.hook: the priest examines in person, never from a distance
397.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on judging others draws on Pirkei Avot's advice to judge every person favorably and not to judge another until you stand in their place, and some teachers pair Tazria with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzara'at, the affliction the rabbis read as harmful speech made visible. Your line was words show on the skin. Did you catch a sentence before it left? Today, who decides. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

A rumor reaches you: so-and-so has really changed, and not for the better. You haven't seen them in a year. You've heard it from two people, maybe three. By dinner, it's easy to half believe it. Leviticus 13 imagines a camp where a mark appears on someone's skin. Everyone can see it. Neighbors could whisper. Family could guess. But the text gives the call to exactly one person, and it gives that person one instruction before anything else.
screen: `A RUMOR REACHES YOU.` → `EVERYONE CAN SEE THE MARK.` → `ONE INSTRUCTION FIRST.`

segments.voice: Start with where the person goes. The text says: when someone has a rising, a scab or a bright spot on the skin, they are brought to Aaron the priest or one of his sons. Not to the neighbors. Not to the group. To someone whose job is to look carefully. Then the priest looks. The Hebrew verb ra'ah, to see, comes again and again in this chapter. The priest looks at the spot. Has the hair in it turned white? Does it seem deeper than the skin? Only after looking does he say a word. There's no ruling from across the camp, no verdict by report. The looking has rules, too. The Mishnah says the priest doesn't examine in the early morning or the evening, or indoors, or on a cloudy day, because in poor light a dull spot can look bright. And not at noon, when a bright one can look dull. Even good eyes need good light. And nobody judges their own. The Mishnah also says a person may examine anyone's affliction except his own, and one opinion adds: or a close relative's. We're bad judges of what's too close to us. Put together, it's a whole ethic of looking. Come close. Look yourself. Wait for the right light. And step aside when you can't see straight. Some teachers carry it far beyond skin: to every time we're tempted to decide about a person from a distance.
screen: `BROUGHT TO THE PRIEST.` · `RA'AH: THE PRIEST MUST SEE.` · `NOT AT DUSK, NOT ON A CLOUDY DAY.` · `NO ONE EXAMINES THEIR OWN.` · then, large: `LOOK, DON'T ASSUME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look carefully before judging. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've formed an opinion about from a distance: from a story, a post, a single bad moment. Ask yourself three of the priest's questions. Have I actually seen this, or heard it? Am I looking in good light, or when I'm tired and annoyed? Am I too close to judge fairly? Then hold your opinion a little more loosely, until you can look again. The bell holds the time.
Tazria. The portion where the priest must come close and look for himself, in good light, before he says anything at all.
Your line: look, don't assume. Today, before you repeat a judgment about someone, find out one thing for yourself. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

398.title: Tazria: wait seven days (Leviticus 13:4–6)
398.hook: when unsure, the priest waits a week and looks again
398.howItsDone: Pirkei Avot is traditionally studied on Shabbat afternoons in the summer, and its first advice is to be deliberate in judgment, and Jewish courts traditionally avoid rushing a verdict.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Tazria, the priest had to come close and look. Your line was look, don't assume. Did you find out one thing for yourself? Today, what the priest does when looking isn't enough. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

An email sent at eleven at night can read very differently at nine the next morning. So can a verdict on someone made on their worst day, before their next week has a chance to prove it wrong. Speed feels like decisiveness. Sometimes it's just impatience wearing a suit. The priest in Leviticus 13 has looked carefully, in good light. And sometimes he still can't tell. The spot is white, but it isn't deeper than the skin. The hair hasn't turned. It could go either way. The Torah tells him exactly what to do with not knowing.
screen: `SENT AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `THE PRIEST CAN'T TELL.` → `WHAT TO DO WITH NOT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Here's the instruction. When the signs are unclear, the priest shuts the person away for seven days. The Hebrew verb is hisgir, to shut in or close up. He doesn't declare them unclean. He doesn't declare them clean. He waits. Then comes a second look. On the seventh day the priest looks again. If the spot has spread, now he knows. If it hasn't, he waits another seven days and looks a third time. Only then, if it has faded and stayed put, is the person declared clean, washes their clothes, and goes home. Two weeks, at most, in this passage. The waiting protects two things. A hasty verdict of unclean would send someone outside the camp for nothing. A hasty clean would miss something real. The week is a kindness to both the person and the truth. The Torah builds in time because first looks can be wrong, even an expert's. Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the sages, opens with the chain of tradition from Sinai, and the first advice in it is for judges: be deliberate in judgment. Slow down. The priest with his calendar is a picture of that advice. Not stuck forever in maybe, and not rushing to certainty either. A set time, and then a fresh look. A week is long enough for a lot of things to show what they really are.
screen: `HISGIR: SHUT AWAY SEVEN DAYS.` · `THE SEVENTH DAY: LOOK AGAIN.` · `A KINDNESS TO PERSON AND TRUTH.` · `BE DELIBERATE IN JUDGMENT.` · then, large: `LOOK AGAIN IN A WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait before one decision. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you've been about to decide quickly. A reply, a purchase, a judgment about someone, a plan to quit something. Ask: is this clear, or am I unsure and pretending not to be? If you're unsure, give it a date, like the priest. Not forever. A week, or even one night. Picture yourself looking again then, with fresh eyes. The bell holds the time.
Tazria. The portion where an unsure priest waits seven days, looks again, and only then decides.
Your line: look again in a week. Today, put one decision you're unsure about on your calendar for seven days from now. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

399.title: Tazria: pray for the one outside (Leviticus 13:45–46)
399.hook: the afflicted cries "unclean"; the Talmud says so that others will pray for him (Shabbat 67a)
399.howItsDone: In many synagogues, during the Torah reading, the congregation says the mi sheberakh prayer for the sick, naming people who are ill, often with their Hebrew name and their mother's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday the priest waited a week before deciding. Your line was look again in a week. Did one decision get a date instead of a guess? Today, the end of Tazria, and a cry from outside the camp. Day three hundred ninety-nine.

It's one of the loneliest pictures in the Torah. Someone has been declared to have tzara'at. Their clothes are torn, their hair left loose, their lip covered, the signs of a mourner. They live alone, outside the camp. And when anyone approaches, they have to call out a word. Read plainly, it sounds like a warning label: stay back. That's how many readers have heard it. The Talmud hears something else in the same cry.
screen: `TORN CLOTHES, LOOSE HAIR.` → `ALONE, OUTSIDE THE CAMP.` → `A CRY, OR A WARNING?`

segments.voice: The verses, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: the person shall cry, "Unclean, unclean." And: "he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his dwelling be." In tractate Shabbat, the rabbis ask why he has to announce it at all. Their answer: so that he makes his pain known to many, and many will ask for mercy for him. The cry isn't only keep away. It's also: I'm here, I'm suffering, remember me. That changes what the camp can do. The person outside can't come in. But the people inside can still pray, if they pray, and they can remember. The boundary stays, and the bond stays too. Jewish practice carries this forward in a prayer called the mi sheberakh for the sick, said at the Torah reading, where names of people who are ill are spoken aloud so the whole congregation holds them. Some people ask to have their own name read. In this tradition, telling others isn't weakness. It's how you let them carry you a little. And the cry closes a hard week. Aaron's sons died and Aaron grieved, first in silence, then with reasons Moses accepted. Shemini ended with kadosh, holy in the everyday. Tazria began with a birth, then tzara'at, a priest who must look, and a priest who waits. And now a person outside the camp, whose cry asks the camp to pray.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone isolated. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is outside the camp right now. Sick at home. In a hospital. Grieving alone. Far away, or cut off, or just lonely in a full house. Say their name to yourself. If you pray, you can ask for mercy for them in your own words, or with a prayer you know. If you don't, hold them in mind with care for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Tazria. The portion that ends with a person crying out from outside the camp, so that others will pray for them.

Your line: pray for the one outside. Today, if something is weighing on you, tell one person, the way the cry lets the camp know, and let them hold it with you. Day three hundred ninety-nine, and another week behind you.
